distractors.reason: Nothing in the passage is about taste; 'tiny sips' points to running out, not to the water tasting bad.
Water warming up hours into a hike is a real experience, so a weak reader who skims past 'plenty' and 'tiny sips' will pick it.
It explains why the supply got smaller, so students who sense 'getting less' but miss that the cause is drinking will choose it.
Kids link 'fancy' with 'expensive'; this is a typical mistake from connotation.
A birthday card with pop-up flowers feels cheerful, so students who go by mood instead of meaning pick it.
'Priya made' is right in the sentence; students match the context detail instead of the word.
A goldfish doing a trick is amazing, and a raised eyebrow is often read as surprise.
'Show me. Then do it again.' sounds demanding, so it gets read as impatient.
'Amazed' already draws the surprise misreading; nothing about the sister's flat, demanding reply sounds excited.
Students who read quickly attach the word to the 'five minutes' sentence or miss the contrast with Owen.
Doing chores is helping, so a typical student who guesses from the general situation picks it.
Nothing in the passage suggests pride; even weak students would not get here from towel-folding.
Slippery old boards are a safety reason to close a bridge, so it fits the outcome sentence.
A town would not close a bridge for squeaking, and students see that the boards had to be replaced.
Old untended wood drying out sounds right to a weak reader as a kind of aging.

distractors.option: as an adverb that tells where
distractors.reason: The clause starts with 'where', and students are taught that 'where' words are adverbs; this is the classic error.

distractors.option: as an adjective that describes Room 12
distractors.reason: The clause sits nowhere near Room 12 and plainly does not describe it; this answer has no pull.

distractors.option: as a noun that is the subject
distractors.reason: A student who knows it is a noun clause but cannot sort subject from object will take the first noun role offered.
It is the most familiar correlative pair, and students miss that 'so ... rented a tent' needs a negative.
It sounds natural at the start of the sentence; students who don't read through to the result clause pick it.
Mismatching 'neither' with 'or' is a very common real error at this age.
The coach is speaking, and students slip into the general 'you'; this pronoun shift shows up constantly in student writing.
Plural 'muscles' and a group of players pull students toward 'their'; it is a common shift away from 'we'.
'We' is right in the clause and the muscles are clearly the team's; few would assign them to the coach.

distractors.option: Dripping with melted cheese, Marco carried the pizza to the table.
distractors.reason: This is the textbook dangling modifier and the exact sentence shape students write themselves.

distractors.option: Marco carried, dripping with melted cheese, the pizza to the table.
distractors.reason: Splitting the verb from its object sounds broken; nobody writes or chooses this.

distractors.option: Marco carried the pizza to the table, dripping with melted cheese.
distractors.reason: A tacked-on ending modifier sounds natural, and it is the most common misplacement students miss.
Sentence 3 contains 'instead of five', so quick readers match the word that echoes it.
It is students' default 'add another fact' transition, used whether or not the logic fits.
The time setting ('every day at lunch') makes a time transition seem to fit to students who miss the cause-effect link.
